extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychoanalysis, literary/theory of humor, and clinicians interested in Freudian theories of defense and humor
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Sigmund Freud's 1928 criteria for 'humour' to determine whether a response qualifies as 'humor proper' — focusing on ego/super-ego/reality relations, economy of affect, and conscious, rebellious triumph of the ego. Includes distinctions from jokes and the comic and diagnostic questions for assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining structure: three parties (ego, super-ego, reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour proper has three parties internally arranged in the same person: The Ego — confronts a situation that ought to provoke pain, terror, or grief; The Super-ego — instead of judging the ego severely, addresses it kindly, almost paternally; The reality — the threatening situation itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The super-ego normally is a harsh critic but in humor speaks with a benevolent parental voice, reframing the world as 'nothing but a game for children' and thereby allowing the ego to take a comic stance toward an actual threat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core criterion: humour as rebellious triumph of the ego and pleasure principle
rubrics_metrics.description: "Humour is not resigned; it is rebellious. It signifies the triumph not only of the ego, but also of the pleasure principle, which is strong enough to assert itself here in the face of the adverse real circumstances."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor is defined by a conscious, defiant facing of painful reality in which the pleasure principle asserts itself — this triumphant stance is central to qualifying a reaction as 'humour proper.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement: genuinely distressing real situation
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuinely distressing real situation — not invented, not hypothetical. Genuine threat, loss, indignity, or pain must be present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of an actual, immediate source of suffering or danger is necessary; purely fanciful, trivial, or hypothetical predicaments do not ground 'humour' in Freud's sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement: presence of mind to take a comic stance
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of mind to take a comic stance toward it — refusing to be overwhelmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The subject must consciously adopt a framing that refuses crushing affect; spontaneity alone isn't enough if the stance does not acknowledge and confront the distress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement: speaker performs parental super-ego role
rubrics_metrics.description: A speaker who plays the parental super-ego role — speaking down at the ego with reassuring detachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The humorous utterance must come from a position that comforts the ego (a kindly, almost paternal voice) rather than from contempt or derision; this internal 'reframe' enables the saving of affect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement: economy of affect
rubrics_metrics.description: An economy of affect — the painful emotion that should have been spent is saved, and that saving is the source of pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central to Freud's account: the pleasure of humor arises because affect that would normally be expended in pain is conserved. Assess whether the response clearly conserves affect rather than merely masking or displacing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm/example: gallows humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: The man being led to the gallows on a Monday remarks, 'Well, the week's starting nicely.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a prototype: real situation = imminent execution; ego's normal response = terror/despair; super-ego reframe = it's just an inconvenient Monday; economy = despair not spent, producing sublime pleasure. The example illustrates all core requirements in one instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing dimension: energy economized and source of pleasure (humour vs joke vs comic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison table: Joke — energy economized = inhibition; Pleasure source = forbidden content slips past censor. Comic — energy economized = ideation; Pleasure source = less mental work than expected. Humor — energy economized = affect; Pleasure source = painful feeling not spent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an utterance, determine which kind of psychic economy is operative: if affect is being conserved and the pleasure derives from surviving real pain, classify as humour rather than joke or comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: not mere wit at someone else's expense
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere wit at the expense of someone else (this is jokes, not humor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the pleasure is derived from an aggressive sally that slips forbidden content past a censor or humiliates another, it is a joke; it lacks the ego-super-ego-reality structure and economy of affect required for 'humour proper.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: not light absurdities without real distress
rubrics_metrics.description: Light absurdities that involve no real distress (this is the comic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playful incongruities or benign absurd situations that do not confront genuine suffering are classified as the comic, not humour, because they economize ideation, not affect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: not cynicism or denial of the threat
rubrics_metrics.description: Cynicism or denial of the threat (humor acknowledges the threat — only then can it transcend it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the response minimizes, denies, or cynically dismisses the reality rather than acknowledging it and reframing from a parental detachment, it fails Freud's criterion for humour and is psychologically different (often defensive in other, less healthy ways).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification: humor as a high-level defense mechanism (conscious and salutary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud calls humor 'one of the highest of the defensive processes.' Unlike repression (which is unconscious and pathological) or sublimation (which redirects), humor faces the unbearable squarely and refuses to suffer it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To qualify as this high defense, the humor must be conscious, confront the painful reality, and transform suffering into a pleasurable saving of affect without self-deception; this distinguishes healthy humor from pathological defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic checklist/questions for assessing humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagnostic questions: Is there a real, present source of pain or threat? Does the speaker acknowledge it rather than deny it? Is the comic stance taken from a position of momentary parental detachment? Does the audience feel both the pain and the relief of refusing to be crushed by it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions as an applied rubric: positive answers to all suggest 'humour proper' per Freud; negative answers point toward jokes, the comic, cynicism, or other responses.
